noticias.titulo: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
noticias.resumen: Anthropic is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, creating a test for the entire industry.
noticias.texto:
Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
- Published
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (Â£1.34 trillion).
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?
In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.
The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.
As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.
"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."
A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.
One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.
Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."
The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.
A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.
Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".
"AI carries real risks," she added.
Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

noticias.titulo: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
noticias.resumen: Orla Guerin speaks to seven people trapped in Taiz by the Houthis who reveal what life is like under siege.
noticias.texto:
'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
- Published
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.
"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."
Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.
Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.
Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.
They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.
On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.
From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.
Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.
Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.
"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.
"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."
She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.
"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.
War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.
Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.
More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.
In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.
A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.
In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.
An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.
Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.
The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."
Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.
They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.
He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".
If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.
"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.
It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.
"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."
He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.
On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.
He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.
The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.
That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.
What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.
He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.
"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".
Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.
How long can the city hold out, I ask.
"Until the population perishes," he replies.
Many in Taiz are resisting.
They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.
They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.
Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.
Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.
When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.
Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (Â£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.
He tells us this fight is different to 2015.
"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."
He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.
But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".
The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.
"They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."
But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.
"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."
The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."
Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.
But could they fight their way in?
Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.
"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.
His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.
Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.
"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."
As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.
"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."
Additional reporting by Wietske Burema and Albaraa Mansoor

noticias.titulo: California targets Nvidia in China AI chip probe
noticias.resumen: The probe by California, where the AI chipmaker has its global headquarters, follows former CEO Jensen Huang's departure.
noticias.texto:
California targets Nvidia in China AI chip probe
- Published
California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.
The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.
The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.
Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.
Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.
Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs â and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates.

noticias.titulo: Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
noticias.resumen: Fiona, who became an internet star after her premature birth in 2017, "fought until she couldn’t anymore", the zoo says.
noticias.texto:
Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
- Published
The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona has died just days after swallowing a knitted hat that slipped into her enclosure.
"It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," the zoo said on Thursday afternoon.
Fiona, who became a social media star after her premature birth in 2017, swallowed the hat about 10 days ago and required emergency care.
The vet staff "tried everything they could to help her" but "it was ultimately too much to overcome", the zoo said.
"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."
Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.
"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.
While she seemed fine at first, her appetite started to decrease a few days later, and the zoo staff tried to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.
An ultrasound before her death showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine. A zookeeper said surgery was not an option for full-grown hippos and "our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own".
The zoo also tried a different approach to attempt to get the hat to pass by encouraging Fiona to stand on a vibration plate platform borrowed from a local horse farm.
"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said.
Fiona was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
Her death is also very premature, with hippos normally living up to 50 years in human care, according to the zoo.
"Although this was not an intentional incident, of which, regrettably, there are many, Fiona's painful death is a tragic reminder that everyone should behave carefully and respectfully around animals," Debbie Metzler, the Managing Director of Captive Wildlife for the animal rights group Peta.
"Peta expects that the zoo will review its protocols to help prevent anything like this from happening again, and we urge every visitor to secure their belongings and never toss objects near an animal's enclosure."
As well as being famous online, Fiona's story inspired an ice cream flavour and a character in Cincinnati's ballet.
Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval said Fiona "was a symbol of perseverance and joy" in the city.
"She brought smiles to so many faces, from kids to parents to visitors from around the world," he wrote on X. "Our city is heartbroken, but we couldn't be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole."

noticias.titulo: Judge finds Thomas Markle mentally fit to stand trial on child abuse charges
noticias.resumen: Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse was deemed competent after an evaluation by a court-appointed psychiatrist.
noticias.texto:
Judge finds Thomas Markle mentally fit to stand trial on child abuse charges
- Published
A judge in Florida has declared Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, to be mentally competent to stand trial for possessing indecent images of children.
The hearing came after an evaluation by a court-appointed psychiatrist conducted on Prince Harry's 82-year-old father-in-law.
Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was ordered to stay in jail pending trial earlier this month after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.
The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home that specialises in dementia. His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles uncovered the abuse material.
Markle appeared in court in Tampa in a wheelchair, and his lawyers did not dispute the court-appointed psychiatrist's finding that he is mentally competent to understand the nature and consequences of the charge against him.
His next court hearing is scheduled for early December, but any trial is expected to take place in California, where the federal charge was filed.
Inside the storage units in Los Angeles the FBI says agents found about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.
In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades.
Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".
He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.
On Monday, police in the Philippines asked prosecutors to charge Markle with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.
Last month, police there obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.
The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018, and he did not attend her wedding in London that same year.
The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

noticias.titulo: Trump posthumously pardons US baseball legend Pete Rose
noticias.resumen: Rose, who died in 2024, was given a lifetime ban from the sport for betting on games but was reinstated last year.
noticias.texto:
Trump posthumously pardons US baseball legend Pete Rose
- Published
US President Donald Trump has posthumously pardoned baseball legend Pete Rose.
"I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday.
Rose, who died in 2024 at the age of 83, pleaded guilty in 1990 to two counts of filing false tax returns. He was also given a lifetime ban from Major League Baseball (MLB) after an investigation revealed he bet on games.
The baseball star was posthumously reinstated to MLB, in which he played for 24 seasons, last year and made eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame.
Trump also said on Thursday that Rose's "record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken".
In fact, Rose accumulated a record 4,256 hits - which MLB defines as a batter striking the baseball into fair territory and reaching base without doing so via an error or a fielder's choice - during his career, which is more than any other player. He played a total of 3,562 games.
According to Trump, Rose "was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Politics, I guess".
The US Constitution gives a sitting president the broad power to grant a pardon, which represents legal forgiveness and ends any further punishment.
Because Rose's pardon was issued after his death, it is largely symbolic and does not change Rose's Hall of Fame status. The Department of Justice (DoJ) typically does not process posthumous pardon applications, though presidents have still issued them.
The BBC has contacted the Hall of Fame and the DoJ for comment.
The US president had previously floated the idea of pardoning Rose in March last year before the MLB reinstated him.
"Major League Baseball didn't have the courage or decency to put the late, great, Pete Rose, also known as 'Charlie Hustle,' into the Baseball Hall of fame," he wrote on Truth Social at the time.
"Now he is dead, will never experience the thrill of being selected, even though he was a FAR BETTER PLAYER than most of those who made it, and can only be named posthumously. WHAT A SHAME," Trump added.
MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred issued a decision in May 2025 that created a pathway for Rose to be eligible to be inducted into the baseball Hall of Fame - a ruling that also applied to 16 other people - as early as 2028.
In August 1989, Rose agreed to the permanent ban from the sport after MLB investigators found that he bet on his team, the Cincinnati Reds, multiple times while he was playing on and managing the team from 1985 to 1987.
In July 1990, after Rose admitted to failing to report $354,968 (Â£271,107) in income over a four-year period, he was sentenced to five months in prison. He also was fined $50,000 and ordered to perform community service at the time.

noticias.titulo: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
noticias.resumen: Hamas condemned the incursion, which the Israeli military said was to dismantle a "terror tunnel", as a "flagrant" ceasefire violation.
noticias.texto:
Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
- Published
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.
Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.
In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.
An image, meanwhile, showed six armoured vehicles, including tanks and bulldozers, around Salah al-Din road.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
Multiple verified videos of the aftermath of the incursion on Thursday showed destruction, earth banks, and heavy vehicle tracks more than 1.2km beyond the Yellow Line.
That is believed to be the furthest Israeli troops have advanced into central Gaza since they occupied the so-called Netzarim Corridor before the ceasefire.
Some residents returned to check their properties following the Israeli withdrawal.
"The entire area has been destroyed, and we honestly do not know what to do," Abd Aliwa told Reuters news agency as he sat beside a pile of rubble.
- Israel moves Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, satellite images show 
  - Published16 January
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".
Gaza health officials said another two people were killed on Thursday by Israeli fire in eastern Gaza City, according to Reuters. There was no immediate comment from the IDF.
At least 1,662 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,710 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry says.

noticias.titulo: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
noticias.resumen: Watch: The BBC's Jonathan Beale joins Ukrainian forces taking the battle below ground and out of sight of Russian drones.
noticias.texto:
Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region.
The BBC is the first international broadcaster to enter the pipeline where this subterranean battle is taking place.
With a diameter of just over a metre there's enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line â and which are making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
The BBC's defence correspondent Jonathan Beale reports from near Kupyansk, where he went underground with the 13th Khartiia Operational Brigade.

noticias.titulo: Parents jailed for torture and death of four-year-old girl found along French motorway in 1987
noticias.resumen: Inass Touloub's body was found along the A10 road in 1987, bearing marks of abuse, and was not identified until 2018.
noticias.texto:
Parents jailed for torture and death of four-year-old girl in France in 1987
- Published
The mother of a four-year-old girl killed in central France and found along a motorway almost 40 years ago has been sentenced to 20 years in prison.
Halima El Bakhti, 72, was found guilty on Tuesday of "torture and acts of barbarity resulting in death without the intent to kill", French media reports.
The girl's father, 74-year-old Ahmed Touloub, was handed a 15-year sentence as an accomplice.
Four-year-old Inass Touloub was found along the A10 road in SuÃ¨vres in the Loir-et-Cher department on 11 August 1987. Her body bore multiple marks of abuse, including human bite marks, broken bones and burns with an iron.
She was buried in an unmarked grave near the location where her body was found. Unidentified for three decades, she was known only as the "Little Martyr of the A10".
Then, in 2018, she was identified after the DNA of her brother â tested in an unrelated case â matched with hers, leading to the arrest of their parents.
The trial took place in Loir-et-Cher Assize Court from 2 November, with the verdict delivered on Tuesday after several hours of deliberation.
During the trial, prosecutor AnaÃ¯s Allio emphasised that "not a single part of Inass's body was spared", and recalled the "sense of vertigo that overcame us all" upon viewing the "unbearable photographs" from the autopsy, France Info reports.
The jury concluded that the child's mother was suffering from impaired judgement at the time of the girl's death, which reduced the maximum potential sentence.
French media outlet France Info described the two defendants as sitting stoically in chairs before the court with their heads bowed as the reasoning behind the verdict was read out.
El Bakhti and Touloub have 10 days to appeal the verdict.
Inass's death sparked one of France's biggest ever investigations, with the girl's photograph posted in public places and an alert sent to more than 30 countries.

noticias.titulo: William and Kate meet PM Modi as they wrap up India tour
noticias.resumen: The meeting in New Delhi was a late addition to the royal couple's India visit, which also included their appearance at the annual Earthshot Prize
noticias.texto:
William and Kate meet PM Modi as they wrap up India tour
- Published
The Prince and Princess of Wales have met India's prime minister as they ended their three-day visit to the country.
Narendra Modi thanked Prince William for bringing his Earthshot prize to the country during the couple's first international tour since 2022.
It comes a day after the royal couple gave out Â£1m prizes to winners of the environmental award, which was founded by the prince and remains one of his biggest personal projects.
Catherine also visited a maternity hospital, where she comforted a grieving mother who lost a baby after giving birth to premature twin girls.
On Wednesday, William and Catherine travelled from Mumbai to capital New Delhi for the final leg of their trip.
During a meeting at Modi's private residence, a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the royals and Modi discussed the "strength and importance of the UKâIndia bilateral relationship, reflecting on the deep and enduring ties between the two countries and the opportunities to strengthen their partnership in the years ahead".
The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and saying how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit.
Modi called it a "pleasure" to meet them, and said he looks forward to "further strengthening" the UKâIndia partnership for the "shared prosperity of the people of our nations and the wider world".
When Prince William announced earlier this year that The Earthshot Prize ceremony was going to be held in India for the first time, he highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.
The royal spokesperson said that the meeting with Modi touched on the success of the ceremony in Mumbai, and India's "growing leadership in environmental innovation".
The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted this year by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known filmmakers.
The couple last met the Indian prime minister on their official visit to India in 2016.
Ahead of their meeting with Modi on Wednesday, William met with film stars during a visit to a film production company, while Catherine visited a maternity hospital, where she met grieving mother Jyoti Karande.
Karande, whose other child remains in intensive care, is receiving treatment in the post-partum ward at Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital.
Catherine told the 29-year-old: "Stay strong. Well done. You've clearly been very, very brave."
William and Catherine's first official overseas trip in four years was short, but allowed them to combine personal projects - like Earthshot - with diplomacy.
As the future king and queen, they are viewed as a valuable diplomatic asset by the UK government.
And with Catherine recovering well and back on international duties following her cancer treatment, visits of a similar kind can be expected to fill their calendar.
  - Published11 November
  - Published25 October

noticias.titulo: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
noticias.resumen: Bahrain says it was also attacked by Iran following a US air strike on the Iranian island of Qeshm in the Gulf on Tuesday.
noticias.texto:
Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
- Published
Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.
The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.
It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.
The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.
The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.
Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.
- Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump 
  - Published1 day ago
- Trump says US taking 'very seriously' any Iranian plot against Washington 
  - Published2 days ago
- Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack 
  - Published4 days ago
On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.
The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law".
"The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.
Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".
The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.
Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".
The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.
Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran.
"If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.
On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.
Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.
In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.
Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".
At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

noticias.titulo: Ghana's new $60m presidential jet sparks public outrage
noticias.resumen: The purchase has sparked outrage over its cost as many Ghanaians struggle with rising cost of living.
noticias.texto:
Ghana's new $60m presidential jet sparks public outrage
- Published
Ghana's government has defended its purchase of a new presidential jet amid criticism over its cost, as many citizens continue to struggle with the high cost of living.
The $60m (Â£46m) French-made Falcon 6X has sparked a political row, with opposition politicians accusing President John Mahama's administration of misplaced priorities.
But the government says the purchase is justified, arguing that Ghana's improving economy makes the aircraft affordable and is needed to replace an ageing presidential jet.
The controversy comes as Mahama's administration seeks to demonstrate an economic recovery after years of financial difficulties that forced Ghana to seek IMF assistance.
- Can Ghana's new president meet the voters' high expectations? 
  - Published7 January 2025
Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.
Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.
The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase.
While in the opposition, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet, prompting questions about why his administration has now gone head with the purchase.
Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the government's priorities, saying the expenditure came at a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living and youth unemployment remained alarmingly high.
"What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed," Jinapor added.
He accused the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) of hypocrisy, recalling how its senior figures had strongly opposed proposals for a new presidential aircraft when they were in opposition.
Jinapor also called for greater transparency over the procurement process, how the purchase was financed and the government's justification for the expenditure.
The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs.
"This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted.
But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.
Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle.
Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties.
"We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.
He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF.
"The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.
Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.
Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.
He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation.
"When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (Â£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.
The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.
But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air".
"There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.
He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.
The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.
The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.
Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.
Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin, an economist at the University of Ghana said that while the president's safety was paramount, the timing of the purchase was difficult to justify amid severe austerity measures, high unemployment and widespread infrastructure challenges.
"The timing makes it a bit difficult to understand," he told the BBC, adding that the government should provide a cost-benefit analysis explaining why buying the jet was preferable to leasing one and how the decision serves Ghana's interests.
Additional reporting by Thomas Naadi in Accra

noticias.titulo: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to be US Speaker of the House
noticias.resumen: The nomination sets him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber when Democrats take control of the House in January.
noticias.texto:
Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to be US Speaker of the House
- Published
Democrats in the US House of Representatives officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, setting him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber.
The House will elect its new Speaker on 3 January, when the next term begins and Democrats will be in the majority.
His election to the powerful position - the Speaker is in line to succeed the president after the vice-president - is widely expected. Should he win, Jeffries will preside over his party's largest House majority in years and benefit from the Senate also being under Democrats' control.
Jeffries told reporters after the vote that the nomination was "a high honour and a distinct privilege".
As of Wednesday, Democrats will hold at least 257 seats in the House next year, which is well beyond the 218 needed for a majority. Seven races from the recent midterm elections are still uncalled.
Jeffries, who represents a district in New York, was re-elected as the party leader in a 251-11 closed-door vote on Wednesday. He has served as minority leader since 2023.
The Congressional Black Caucus, currently made up of only Democratic House members, noted the potential history-making moment when Jeffries takes the helm of the House.
"The American people, largely driven by turnout among Black communities, particularly across the south, have trusted us to make Washington work for them," said the committee's chair, Yvette Clarke, in a statement. "Now, it is our charge and responsibility to do all we can to deliver on their faith."
Despite overwhelming support in Wednesday's vote , Jeffries faced a handful of holdouts from new members in the party's left wing, who have said the party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections is a sign voters want change.
"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes in this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of our leadership," seven incoming lawmakers, including fellow New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, said in a statement.
All congressional Democrats are gearing up for clashes with the White House once they officially take control in January.
President Donald Trump, a Republican, has signalled a willingness to work with Democrats on some issues, but has also pledged to use his veto power to reject legislation he does not like.
Trump's opposition could make it hard for Democrats to deliver on their campaign promises to address affordability and pass other reforms.
At a news conference following the vote on Wednesday, Jeffries pledged that House Democrats would "fight to lower the high costs of groceries and gas and housing", and "make healthcare affordable for every single American".
Though the party will have a large enough majority to weather defections on must-pass legislation, Jeffries will still have to navigate internal ideological divisions that have grown particularly sharp over US support of Israel and Americans' rising healthcare costs.
Many incoming Democrats, including members of the Democratic Socialists of America, won their elections by challenging the party establishment.
The Congressional Progressive Caucus, from the party's left wing, congratulated Jeffries on the nomination, adding they would "continue conversations with Leader Jeffries to ensure Democrats deliver a bold agenda for working people".
Along with shepherding legislation, Jeffries as Speaker will also have to manage the complex array of investigations that Democrats plan to launch into Trump, his family, and cabinet members now that they have regained control of the chamber's oversight powers.
Rounding out their party leadership team, House Democrats also elected Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as majority leader, Pete Aguilar of California as majority whip, and Joe Neguse of Colorado as assistant speaker.
  - Published4 November
  - Published5 November

noticias.titulo: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
noticias.resumen: The BBC's Samira Hussain breaks down the AI company's first day as a publicly traded company, as shares closed up 17%.
noticias.texto:
How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, closed 17% higher on its first day as a publicly traded company. Shares closed at $97.17, giving the company a market valuation of around $1.77 trillion, after briefly surpassing $2 trillion during trading.
The debut came as the wider technology sector fell 2.4%, raising questions about investor confidence in the AI boom.
The BBC's Samira Hussain breaks down Anthropic's first day on the stock market.

noticias.titulo: From premature baby to social media star - Famed hippo Fiona dies
noticias.resumen: The beloved hippopotamus died days after swallowing a knitted hat that accidentally got into her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo.
noticias.texto:
From premature baby to social media star - Famed hippo Fiona dies
The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona has died just days after swallowing a knitted hat that slipped into her enclosure.
Fiona was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species. She reached 1,000 lbs in 2018.
Over the years, Fiona became a favourite among visitors and a star on social media. This video captures moments from her life, from her early days as a calf to celebrating her fifth birthday and receiving treatment just a few days ago.
Read more about Fiona here.

noticias.titulo: Cumin-laced fizzy sodas are giving cola giants a tough fight in India
noticias.resumen: Cumin-laced sodas are capturing a bigger market share in India as demand for homegrown flavours goes up.
noticias.texto:
Cumin-laced fizzy sodas are giving cola giants a tough fight in India
- Published
It began as an impromptu kitchen experiment.
Saurabh Munjal, Nikhil Doda and Saurabh Bhutna - three cousins in India's north-western Punjab state - were messing about at home post dinner one evening, when Doda casually brewed up a tangy cumin-flavoured fizzy soda using regular pantry ingredients.
They enjoyed its earthy, piquant taste so much that they decided to explore options to sell it commercially.
Cumin-laced sodas had always been sold at street-side stalls in India, but it was a broken market of local companies. Not many had built a carbonated beverage brand around the flavour.
The trio persuaded their families to invest some capital and launched Lahori Zeera in 2017. Zeera is the Hindi name for cumin.
Almost a decade on, the drink has become a bit of a sensation in India, challenging the entrenched monopoly of global cola giants, especially in the all-important mass-market ten-rupee ($0.11; Â£0.078) beverage category - it will close this year with revenues of $115-120m.
Its popularity reflects a growing consumer preference for distinctly Indian flavours and drinks perceived to be more healthy, say analysts.
Lahori Zeera is one of several cumin-flavoured soda brands that have mushroomed across the country over the past decade.
There's Jeeru from Mumbai-based Xotik Frujus, Campa Jeera from billionaire Mukesh Ambani-owned Campa Cola and at least half-a-dozen other variants from regional players including Fizz Jeera Masala from House of Bindu.
Bindu launched their cumin soda nearly 25 years ago, but sales were flat until some years ago, according to Megha Shankar, a director with the company.
"Now it is the fastest growing category among carbonated beverages," Shankar told the BBC. "Its contribution to our revenues has doubled from 20% to 40% in the last five years."
Soaring demand for the product has pushed House of Bindu to widen its footprint across the country, after being largely based in southern India for over two decades.
Parle Agro, external, one of India's oldest consumer brands, also rolled out its own cumin soda brand Dhishoom nationally last year after exclusively selling it in rural markets since 2012.
Online orders for these fizzy drinks, meanwhile, were up 900% this summer according to a report from one of India's online delivery companies.
The cumin frenzy is reshaping India's non-alcoholic beverages market, which was valued at $32 billion in 2024 and projected to double by 2033.
According to a report from Kotak Mutual Fund earlier this year, Lahori Zeera, Campa and other smaller challengers - now dubbed as India's "ethnic beverages market" - collectively doubled their share of India's carbonated soft-drinks market to around 15% by September last year, while the combined market share of Coca-Cola and PepsiCo fell from roughly 93% to 85%.
"This is a "Jio moment" for beverages. Just as telecom incumbents bled market share when data prices crashed, beverage incumbents are bleeding volume," the Kotak report said, drawing an analogy to the disruption caused by the entry of Reliance-owned Jio Telecom in India's telecoms market in 2016.
"In global markets,â¯establishedâ¯duopolies rarely lose more than 1-2% share annually; anâ¯8% swingâ¯in less than a year is a structural disruption."
Saurabh Munjal, CEO of Archian Foods which manufactures Lahori Zeera, told the BBC that the company has "always been in a situation where we are sold out each year. We've doubled our capacity to 1.2 million bottles per day last year and are still unable to meet demand".
For decades, the colas have had a dominant presence in India, appealing to the aspirational part of the population as lifestyle products that were cool to consume.
With millions of dollars in marketing budgets splashed out on billboards, Bollywood stars and cricket championships, they sold a very western idea of hydration to India, says Munjal.
But home-grown brands are now mounting a serious challenge with a combination of smart distribution, attractive pricing and a turn towards nostalgic Indian flavours such as cumin, raw mango, kokum fruit and tamarind.
Munjal says that for long, there has been a tendency among consumer brands in India to either westernise Indian products or "Indianise" western products. But with Lahori Zeera, which uses the tagline "apna desi thanda", meaning India's own cold drink, his desire is to change that.
Shankar says her brand has also recently launched a zero-sugar version of their cumin soda to capture the growing market for healthier non-cola drinks.
This success notwithstanding, sustaining this winning trajectory will not be easy for these ethnic beverage brands, say analysts. The very factors that propelled their rise could also limit growth.
"The million-dollar question is how big can the cumin-flavoured drink market become. And I suspect it won't become as big as the colas," Rajiv Agarwal, a professor at Mumbai-based SP Jain Institute of Management, who advises family businesses on strategies to succeed against multi-national corporations, told the BBC.
The 10-rupee price point, which accounts for the bulk of sales volumes in India's cumin-flavoured carbonated drinks market, is another double-edged sword.
While it has driven up sales, the soaring cost of plastic, packaging, sugar and other raw material amid the global energy shock could start to hit margins, which are already very thin.
Raising prices, meanwhile, could affect volumes, forcing brands to further reduce bottle sizes, something the cola companies had resorted to a few years ago.
Then there is always the threat of bigger, deep-pocketed players coming in to disrupt the category.
"Competition is extremely aggressive," says Agarwal. And the established global players are better organised in terms of systems, processes, distribution channels and bottling arrangements.
Coca Cola, which had acquired the cumin-flavoured Rimzim brand in the 1990s, is strengthening its play in this category and reportedly doubled production last year.
But the challenges haven't deterred the ambitions of the homegrown players.
"Indian flavours need to find a global spotlight," says Munjal, who is looking to tap the global market in the coming years.
"For generations, we've grown up drinking colas of the world, but I hope the next generations will drink the zeeras of India."

noticias.titulo: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
noticias.resumen: African countries at the UN climate summit in Turkey are demanding more funding from developed nations to help them cope with climate change.
noticias.texto:
More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
- Published
In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.
A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.
"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.
"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."
Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.
Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.
In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.
Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.
"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.
He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.
"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.
After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.
"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."
A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.
While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.
These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.
"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.
"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."
The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (Â£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.
The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.
The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.
But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.
"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.
He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.
Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones.
"If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.
- 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El NiÃ±o with floods predicted 
  - Published11 November
- A really simple guide to climate change 
  - Published6 November
Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.
The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.
Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.
Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.
Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.
But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?
"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam.
"Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."
Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support.
"The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.
She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience.
"When countries lack adequate adaptation planning and, more importantly, the resources to implement those plans, governments are forced into a cycle of responding to disasters instead of preventing or reducing their impacts," said Amos Wemanya, senior climate adviser at Power Shift Africa.
"Instead of investing in early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, water security and flood protection, scarce public resources are repeatedly diverted towards emergency relief and reconstruction. This costs more over time and leaves communities increasingly vulnerable."
African negotiators acknowledge that adaptation plans help countries prioritise investments and attract funding, but argue that their absence should not be used to deny them financial support.
"Of course, having a comprehensive NAP helps countries prioritise investments and prepare proposals for climate finance," said Mahlet Eyassu Melkie, a senior strategic adviser to Ethiopia's COP32 presidency.
"But Africa's adaptation financing needs are based on scientific assessments, climate vulnerability, national priorities and regional estimates â not simply on whether every country has submitted a particular planning document."
The UN Development Programme, which has helped more than 45 countries prepare their plans, said NAPs can help governments mobilise international support and coordinate climate action.
Fred Njehu, a Pan-African political strategist at Greenpeace Africa, said their absence could nevertheless create significant obstacles.
"It is fair to acknowledge that missing adaptation plans act as a major functional barrier that severely bottlenecks the speed, volume and quality of international funding a country can access," he said.
But having a plan does not guarantee the money needed to implement it.
"Even countries that have completed their NAPs have not received money anywhere near what they require for implementation of their adaptation plans," Apiny said.
Kenya offers an example of how adaptation measures can help communities cope with climate pressures.
In the country's arid and semi-arid south-east, concrete sand dams slow the flow of seasonal rivers, allowing sand to accumulate and store water underground. Communities can access it during dry periods using hand pumps or by scooping it out.
UK charity Sand Dams Worldwide and its local partner, the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, said they had built about 1,300 such dams, improving access to water as droughts become more frequent and intense.
But many vulnerable communities elsewhere on the continent are still waiting for similar interventions.
Back in drought-hit Karamoja, Lobur wonders how different things might have been if farmers had access to small-scale irrigation schemes.
"We do have some underground water sources in some places. If there were proper plans and programmes, we could have tapped them to grow food, but we are having to live in hunger instead," Lobur said.
"My grandmother keeps reminding us how she lost eight children during a famine-like situation in 1982, and we all fear we might perish like that too."
